newsitem.title: UK: N. Irish police find big explosives cache.
newsitem.headline: N. Irish police find big explosives cache.

text.p: Hopes of a truce by IRA guerrillas were dimmer on Monday after police in Northern Ireland found a large quantity of home-made explosives they said was "one step" away from being turned into a bomb.

Around 300 lb (150 kg) of the explosive, a favoured weapon of guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland, was found on Sunday in three plastic bins in a coal shed at the back of a house in the heavily Catholic and Irish nationalist city of Londonderry, police said.
Another two bags of explosive were found as police evacuated 50 houses and searched the area into the night.
"It was just one step away from being fully functional," said a police spokesman. "It was meant to be planted and it was meant to cause death."

Police said they had no idea what had been been the likely target of the bomb and declined to comment on who they believe prepared it, although they said the location of the find pointed to republican guerrillas.

The discovery was announced just hours after Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, appeared to dash hopes of a new IRA ceasefire which would pave the way for his party's admission to Northern Ireland peace talks.

As the British-ruled province recovered from a week of violence sparked by parades by pro-British Protestant groups, Adams said demands that the guerrillas should start handing in their weapons remained a stumbling block.
Adams, responding to Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said in a statement that the surrender of arms held by his guerrilla allies "still remains a major difficulty".

Mowlam had appealed earlier on Sunday for a new ceasefire by the Irish Republican Army (IRA), a move which would win Sinn Fein a seat at peace talks within six weeks, saying: "Let the IRA/Sinn Fein make their decision, the ball is in their court."
But Protestant Unionists loyal to British rule dismissed hopes of a new IRA truce as "wishful thinking".

"The reality is that Sinn Fein/IRA are committed to violence in order to achieve objectives that no democrat can support," said David Trimble, the head of Northern Ireland's biggest pro-British group, the Ulster Unionist party.
Hopes of progress towards peace rose after the Protestant Orange Order scrapped four parades over the weekend that had been routed through Catholic areas and were likely to spark rioting.

The marches, on a day when the Orange Order recalls a 1690 Protestant victory over a Catholic king, were scrapped after the threat of mass counter-demonstrations by Catholics who see the parades as intimidation.

The decision marked a climbdown after Britain decided to allow Protestant marchers to parade along the Catholic Garvaghy Road of Portadown, the site of a bitter standoff last year which sparked province-wide rioting.

Hundreds of other marches went ahead on Saturday, but moderate Catholic nationalist leader John Hume hailed the "moral courge" of the Orange Order for calling off the four flashpoint parades and defusing fears of sectarian strife.
Police said the province was calm in the early hours of Monday.

But tension was once again high after the the explosive find and Adams' statement, which echoed the IRA position that the scrapping of weapons should take place at the end of talks on a settlement between the Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists.
Britain's new Labour government has dropped demands for the IRA to disarm before Sinn Fein can join the talks, but is still insisting that the guerrillas must give up weapons during the talks.
